false_positives.candidate:
History and Origin can panic when search is not configured

`server.History` calls `s.search.History(...)` and `server.Origin` calls `s.search.Origin(...)` without checking whether `s.search` is nil. `NewResourceServer` can leave `s.search` nil when search resources are not configured or when `SearchOptions.Backend` is nil (`newSearchSupport` returns nil, nil). A gRPC History or Origin request in that configuration will dereference a nil pointer and panic. `Search` has a nil guard, but History and Origin do not.

Startup index-build goroutines share and race on the outer err variable

In `searchSupport.init`, each errgroup closure assigns to the outer `err` variable via `_, _, err = s.build(...)` and then returns it. Multiple index-build goroutines run concurrently and write to the same variable, causing a data race. This can also cause one goroutine's error to be overwritten by another goroutine's success, so `Init` may report success even though an index build failed. Each closure should use its own local error variable.

Unsynchronized increment of totalBatchesIndexed in concurrent startup builds

`totalBatchesIndexed++` is executed inside errgroup goroutines without any synchronization. Multiple goroutines can increment the same integer concurrently, which is a data race and can produce an incorrect value in the `namespaced_indexed` span attribute. Use an atomic counter or protect the counter with a mutex.

Events written during initial index build can be missed permanently

`searchSupport.init` builds all initial indexes first and only afterward calls `WatchWriteEvents` to start consuming new events. The resource version returned by `build`/`ListIterator` is discarded. Any writes committed between the initial listing for a namespace and the creation of the watch subscription are not applied to the newly built index. Because startup indexing can take a long time, this creates a potentially large window where the search index can become stale until another write happens for the same resource.

Search event loop does not handle a closed watch channel

The event loop started by `searchSupport.init` receives from the watch channel with `v := <-events` and does not check whether the channel is closed. The SQL backend closes its event channel on shutdown. After closure, this loop receives nil repeatedly and calls `handleEvent` with a nil event, causing a nil-pointer dereference on `evt.Type` or a tight loop. The loop also uses `context.Background()` and has no graceful shutdown path.

Broadcaster pipe does not handle a closed backend event channel

In `server.initWatcher`, the goroutine that pipes backend watch events reads `v := <-events` without checking the channel's ok value and then accesses `v.Type` and `v.ResourceVersion`. If the backend closes the event channel, as the SQL backend does when stopped, this dereferences a nil event and panics, or spins on a closed channel. A closed-channel check and shutdown path are needed.

Constructor leaks resources when Init fails

`NewResourceServer` creates a cancelable context and then calls `s.Init(ctx)`. If `Init` fails, the constructor returns an error without calling the cancel function and without stopping any components that were partially initialized. If lifecycle initialization succeeded, or if `search.init` started its event goroutine before a later watcher failure, those resources and goroutines are leaked on construction failure.

handleEvent can panic when IndexMetrics is nil

`searchSupport.handleEvent` uses `IndexMetrics.IndexedKinds` for ADDED and DELETED events without checking whether `IndexMetrics` is nil. Other code paths guard this global with `if IndexMetrics != nil`. If metrics are not initialized, processing a watch event will panic.

BuildIndex can panic when IndexMetrics is nil

`bleveBackend.BuildIndex` increments `resource.IndexMetrics.IndexTenants` without checking whether `resource.IndexMetrics` is nil. Other parts of the code guard this global, so building an index can panic when metrics are not initialized.

builderCache.get can return a nil DocumentBuilder without error

`builderCache.get` falls back to `s.defaultBuilder` and returns it without error. `newBuilderCache` does not require a default builder unless the configuration list is empty, so for an unregistered group/resource this can return a nil `DocumentBuilder` with a nil error. Callers such as `searchSupport.build` and `searchSupport.handleEvent` then call `BuildDocument` on the nil builder and panic.

Bleve index is not closed when BuildIndex fails after creation

In `bleveBackend.BuildIndex`, if `getAllFields` or the builder callback fails after `bleve.New` or `bleve.NewMemOnly` has created an index, the function returns without closing the newly created `bleve.Index`. For file-backed indexes this leaks file handles and can leave a locked index directory behind.

Poller span is not ended when listLatestRVs fails

In `backend.poller`, a span is started on every poll tick. If `listLatestRVs` returns an error, the code resets the ticker and continues without calling `span.End()`. Repeated failures will leak spans and retain tracing state unnecessarily.

Postgres coverage is skipped for storage server startup test

The integration test now skips all Postgres runs. Since this PR changes startup initialization and indexing behavior, Postgres coverage for the storage server target is lost, and the failure mode that motivated the skip is only annotated with a TODO.

false_positives.candidate:
Strategy close shuts down the factory-shared FixedQueuePool

ResultsStrategyFactory creates one FixedQueuePool in __init__ (result_consumer.py line 133) and reuses it for every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close/terminate/join shuts that pool down, stopping worker threads and closing the queues. Arroyo closes the old strategy on partition revocation/reassignment, so after a rebalance the factory will create new strategies around an already shut-down pool. New messages then cannot be processed, and enqueue attempts may fail or be dropped. The pool lifecycle must match the strategy lifecycle, or the pool must be recreated on each assignment.

Unbounded worker queues provide no backpressure

Each worker queue is created as queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and FixedQueuePool.submit puts items unconditionally. If workers are slower than the consumer—exactly the slow-item case this PR is trying to address—the consumer will keep polling and enqueuing full Kafka payloads without bound. poll() only emits a gauge and does not block or raise. This can cause unbounded memory growth. Use bounded queues, block in submit, or apply backpressure in poll.

Offsets are completed and can be committed even when processing fails

OrderedQueueWorker.run marks the offset complete in finally, so an exception from result_processor still allows the offset to become committable. ResultProcessor.__call__ in result_consumer.py also swallows all exceptions and only logs them. The result is that failed results can be committed and never retried, contradicting the strategy docstring claim that offsets are committed only after successful processing. This can silently drop uptime results. Failures should prevent completion, or be routed to retry/DLQ.

submit() marks offsets complete when it cannot enqueue/process a message

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches all exceptions and, if the message has a BrokerValue, immediately adds and completes the offset. This includes decoder/grouping errors and failures from queue_pool.submit, such as submitting to a shut-down queue. The message is not processed, but its offset becomes committable. That turns transient or operational errors into silent data loss. Errors should be surfaced, retried, dead-lettered, or should block the consumer rather than completing the offset.

OffsetTracker iterates all_offsets while other threads mutate it

OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets iterates list(self.all_offsets.keys()) without a global lock, while add_offset can concurrently insert new partition keys from the consumer thread. Concurrent mutation of the partition dictionary can cause RuntimeError during iteration or inconsistent snapshots. Protect the partition set with a global lock, or copy/modify it under a lock.

Shutdown stops workers before draining queues and join ignores its timeout

FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown = True before shutting down the queues, so each worker exits after finishing its current item instead of draining remaining queued work. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(timeout) calls close() and ignores the timeout, forcibly shutting down the pool. Queued items are dropped on shutdown/rebalance instead of being processed up to the requested timeout. It should wait_until_empty(timeout) and only stop workers after draining or after the timeout expires.

Uses Python 3.13-only queue.ShutDown/Queue.shutdown APIs

OrderedQueueWorker catches queue.ShutDown, and FixedQueuePool.shutdown calls q.shutdown(immediate=False). These APIs were added in Python 3.13. If this consumer runs on an older supported Python version, shutdown will not work correctly: Queue.shutdown will raise AttributeError (caught and logged), workers may never be woken from queue.get(), and exception handling can fail. Add a fallback for older Python versions or explicitly enforce Python 3.13+.

decode_payload asserts on FilteredPayload instead of handling it

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy's decoder type accepts KafkaPayload | FilteredPayload, but ResultsStrategyFactory.decode_payload begins with assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload). Any FilteredPayload message therefore raises AssertionError, which SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit treats as a generic submission error and logs. Filtered payloads should be handled explicitly by returning None so they can be skipped without exception/log spam.

WorkItem retains the full Kafka message though it is unused

WorkItem stores the original Message[KafkaPayload | FilteredPayload], but only partition and offset are used for offset tracking; the message field is never read. With unbounded queues, this unnecessarily retains full Kafka payloads in memory. Remove the unused message field or store only the required metadata.

max_workers is not validated for thread-queue-parallel mode

FixedQueuePool is created with num_queues=max_workers or 20. This treats 0 as 20, but negative values are passed through. A negative num_queues creates no queues and later hash(group_key) % num_queues or queue lookup can fail. Validate that max_workers/num_queues is a positive integer when using thread-queue-parallel.

false_positives.candidate:
Span buffer switches from Redis sets to sorted sets without migration or key namespacing

Existing span-buf:s:* keys created by the previous code are Redis sets. The new code calls ZADD on those keys and the Lua script uses ZCARD/ZUNIONSTORE. If any in-flight segment from the old version exists during deployment, Redis will return WRONGTYPE and processing will fail, causing stuck or dropped spans. A new key prefix, migration, or drain procedure is needed.

ZPOPMIN eviction can remove root spans or other semantically important spans

The script caps each segment at 1000 members by removing the lowest-scored members, where score is end_timestamp_precise. It has no special protection for the segment/root span. If the root span has one of the lowest end timestamps, or a missing/zero timestamp, it can be evicted. The segment may then be marked as having a root span while the root payload is missing, breaking downstream segment semantics.

Redirect resolution depth was reduced to 1000 and can fragment deep traces

The loop follows at most 1000 redirects in the span redirect map. If a redirect chain is longer, the script stops at an intermediate set and stores the span there, which can prevent related spans from being joined into one segment. The previous limit was 10000 and the correctness tradeoff was at least documented; the new lower limit changes behavior for deep traces without tests or migration notes.

SpansBuffer.__reduce__ reconstructs the object with the wrong positional arguments

__reduce__ returns SpansBuffer with (assigned_shards, span_buffer_timeout_secs, span_buffer_root_timeout_secs, redis_ttl). The fourth positional argument of SpansBuffer.__init__ is segment_page_size, not redis_ttl, and max_segment_bytes/max_segment_spans/redis_ttl are not preserved. When SpansBuffer is pickled for multiprocessing, the unpickled buffer will have incorrect configuration.

Flush path no longer enforces a span-count limit

_load_segment_data removed the check that skipped segments larger than max_segment_spans. The Lua script only evicts when new inserts push a set above 1000 members, so pre-existing or otherwise unevicted segments can contain many small spans under max_segment_bytes and be loaded, serialized, and produced in one flush, causing memory/CPU spikes or oversized downstream messages.

Typo assigning queryset.query.order_b leaves ordering unchanged

In build_queryset, when converting an existing descending order to ascending, the code assigns to queryset.query.order_b instead of queryset.query.order_by. The intended ordering change is silently dropped, which can produce incorrect previous-page results for paginators relying on this branch.

No tests cover the new eviction cap or set-to-zset migration behavior

The test changes only add end_timestamp_precise to existing fixtures. There are no tests that insert more than 1000 spans to verify ZPOPMIN eviction, verify that root spans are preserved, or verify behavior when old Redis set keys exist. Given the data-loss and compatibility risks introduced by this PR, these cases need coverage.

false_positives.candidate:
Accidental submodule committed

This PR adds a git submodule named 'sentry-repo' pointing at a commit. That appears unintentional and can break clones, CI, or repository layout. Remove the submodule/gitlink before merging.

Error-focused query detection is a naive substring check

_is_error_focused_query returns true whenever 'event.type:error' appears in the raw request query. This matches negated clauses such as '!event.type:error', mixed queries like 'event.type:error OR event.type:transaction', and text inside quoted values. It also fails to treat '!event.type:transaction' as error-focused. Since this controls whether count() is replaced by sum(sample_weight), it can apply weights to non-error events or miss error-only queries, producing incorrect counts. Parse the search syntax or use the final query string instead.

Eligibility cache can serve stale allowlist decisions and has no wired invalidation

Allowlist eligibility is cached for 60 seconds, but invalidate_upsampling_cache is never called when the 'issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist' option changes. If the allowlist is updated, queries can continue using the old upsampling decision for up to a minute, returning incorrect counts. Include a config version in the cache key or invoke invalidation on option changes.

Only literal count() is transformed and aliasing is forced

The transform only rewrites columns that exactly match 'count()' after lower/strip and rewrites them to 'upsampled_count() as count'. It does not handle aliased forms like 'count() as total', other count variants, or equations. This can leave some count aggregations unupsampled while changing the output alias for others, causing inconsistent API responses for clients expecting the original field name.

Allowlist membership check uses list lookups

_are_all_projects_error_upsampled checks 'project_id in allowlist' where allowlist is a list. On a cache miss this is O(number of queried projects * allowlist size). Convert the allowlist to a set before checking membership.

upsampled_count is exposed as a public query function

The new upsampled_count SnQL function is added without private=True, unlike neighboring internal functions. This may allow API callers to invoke it directly in queries, bypassing the allowlist/error-upsampling checks and potentially exposing sample-weight-derived counts. Mark the function private or gate it appropriately.

upsampled_count does not handle missing/null sample weights

The aggregate is toInt64(sum(sample_weight)). If any event in an allowlisted project has a NULL or unpopulated sample_weight (for example historical events before upsampling metadata existed), those events can contribute zero or nothing to the sum, causing severe undercounting. Use coalesce(sample_weight, 1) or another explicit default unless the schema guarantees a non-NULL weight of 1 for every row.

toInt64 truncates fractional upsampled sums

sample_weight values can be fractional, and sum(sample_weight) may therefore be fractional. Wrapping it in toInt64 truncates rather than rounding, biasing the estimated error count downward. Consider rounding or returning a numeric/float result.

Endpoint tests do not clear or test the upsampling eligibility cache

The tests patch the allowlist option but do not clear the 'error_upsampling_eligible:*' cache entries. Since the eligibility cache lives for 60 seconds, a value cached by one test can affect later tests with the same organization/project IDs, making the suite order-dependent and preventing validation of stale-cache behavior. Clear the cache in setUp or add explicit cache invalidation/staleness tests.

Missing coverage for key upsampling paths

The new tests only cover simple stats requests with 'event.type:error'. They do not cover the errors dataset, top-events paths, RPC paths, aliased/equation count columns, dashboard split queries, or mixed/negated event.type queries. These are the paths where the transform is applied and are likely to regress.

Denial cache key is not scoped by identity type

In Service.Check, permDenialKey is built from namespace, user identifier, action, resource name, and parent folder, but not the identity type. validateSubject permits anonymous and render-service identities, and both can have the identifier "0" (e.g. anonymous:0 and render:0). A denied anonymous check will therefore write a negative cache entry under the same key used by a render:0 check for the same resource. A subsequent renderer check can hit that denial cache entry and return Allowed:false before getRendererPermissions is evaluated, even though the renderer is hard-coded to read all dashboards/folders. Similar cross-identity denials are possible between other identity types if identifiers are not globally unique. The denial cache key should include the identity type, or renderer/anonymous checks should bypass this denial cache.

Negative caching can continue denying access after permission is granted

Service.Check stores a denial in permDenialCache for shortCacheTTL (30 seconds) whenever the database check denies access. There is no invalidation when permissions are added or changed. If a permission is granted immediately after a denial—for example during dashboard/folder creation, permission propagation, or a read-before-write race—subsequent checks can hit the denial cache and keep rejecting the user until the TTL expires. This can reintroduce the same inability to access newly created resources that this PR is trying to fix.

Errors from cached identity lookup are treated as cache misses

getCachedIdentityPermissions can return real errors from GetUserIdentifiers for user/service-account subjects, but Service.Check only proceeds with the cached path when err == nil and otherwise falls through as though it were a cache miss. It then calls getIdentityPermissions, which repeats GetUserIdentifiers. This can duplicate database work during failures, add latency, and emit misleading cache-miss metrics instead of distinguishing cache lookup failures from ordinary cache misses.

This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

false_positives.candidate:
Update invalidation can miss login-cache invalidation because it uses an organization-aware original model

In update(), the original model is fetched via getById(), which wraps the model so isEnabled() also checks whether the linked organization is enabled. registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate() then applies LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate(), which includes the enabled check. If the linked organization is disabled, the original model fails the predicate even though the IDP itself is storage-enabled. An update that makes the IDP unsuitable for login while the organization is disabled (for example setting hideOnLogin or linkOnly to true) can therefore have both original and updated predicates evaluate to false, so no login-cache invalidation is registered. When the organization is later enabled again, stale cached getForLogin results may still include an IDP that should be hidden or link-only. The original state should be evaluated with the raw storage model, or invalidation should be conservative here.

getForLogin does not check invalidation of the requested organization

getForLogin() only checks whether the realm/fetch-mode cache key is invalid. Unlike getByOrganization(), it does not check whether the supplied organizationId itself has been invalidated. If an organization is updated, disabled, removed, or its IDP association changes in a way that registers an organization invalidation, this method can still serve a stale cached list for that organization. Because the cached list is later resolved only by ID, the result may no longer match the requested organization or login availability.

Cached getForLogin results are returned without revalidating login eligibility

After a cache hit, getForLogin() resolves the cached internal IDs and returns them without re-applying LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate() or verifying that each provider still matches the requested FetchMode and organizationId. Correctness therefore depends entirely on invalidations being perfect. Given the update-invalidation issue with organization-aware enabled state and the missing organization invalidation check, this can return providers that are currently disabled, hidden, link-only, or associated with a different organization. Filtering the resolved models before returning would make the cache robust against missed invalidations.

The login cache stores one IdentityProviderListQuery per realm and FetchMode, with internal search keys for each requested organizationId. Every distinct organization ID used in getForLogin is merged into the same cache object. In realms with many organizations, this single cache entry can become large, and each new organization search invalidates and rewrites the whole entry, causing cache churn and potential contention. A per-organization cache key or bounded structure would avoid unbounded growth and repeated invalidation of the shared entry.

broker_public changes on realm-level IDPs may not invalidate ORG_ONLY login cache

registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate() skips invalidation when both old and new models satisfy the login predicate and the organization ID is unchanged. For an IDP with organizationId == null, the predicate is true regardless of the broker_public config. However the default getForLogin(ORG_ONLY, null) query filters by OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC, so changing broker_public on a realm-level IDP can change the ORG_ONLY result set. true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is not rechecked after acquiring the write lock

In GetWebAssets, the cache pointer is checked under RLock, the read lock is released, and then the write lock is acquired without rechecking entryPointAssetsCache. In non-dev mode, multiple concurrent requests during a cold start can all observe a nil cache and proceed past the early return. After one goroutine populates the cache, the others will still reload the manifest and then unconditionally assign entryPointAssetsCache = result. This causes redundant I/O while holding the mutex and, if one of those later reloads fails, it can overwrite a freshly populated valid cache with nil. The code should recheck the cache after acquiring the write lock and return the existing value when appropriate, or use sync.Once/singleflight for initialization.

false_positives.candidate:
Asynchronous legacy writes are derived from the request context

In Create, and similarly in Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection, the background goroutine creates a timeout context from the incoming request context. Request contexts are normally canceled when the HTTP handler returns, so the 10-second timeout does not make the legacy write independent. The legacy operation may be canceled immediately after the API response is sent, causing mode 3 to skip the intended asynchronous legacy write. A detached context, with logger/values copied, should be used instead.

Legacy Create uses the original request object instead of the created object

Mode3.Create passes the original obj to Legacy.Create after Storage.Create has returned created. Storage may assign name, UID, resourceVersion, annotations, or defaults, and created is the canonical object that unified storage accepted. Passing the original object, rather than a deep copy of created, can create a different object in legacy storage or cause concurrent use of a mutable object. This can make legacy storage diverge from unified storage.

Legacy Update reuses the request UpdatedObjectInfo instead of the unified result

Mode3.Update calls Storage.Update with objInfo and then asynchronously calls Legacy.Update with the same objInfo. Legacy.Update will normally evaluate objInfo against the legacy store's current object, so patches, strategic merges, or resource-version-dependent updates can produce a different result or fail. To keep legacy consistent, the legacy update should receive an UpdatedObjectInfo that returns the exact object returned by Storage.Update, preferably a deep copy.

Unordered background goroutines can leave legacy storage inconsistent

Each write operation starts an independent goroutine to write to legacy storage without sequencing, queueing, or per-resource locking. Rapid create/update/delete operations can be applied to legacy out of order, for example a legacy delete can run before a legacy create or an older update can overwrite a newer one. Because mode 3 keeps legacy as a fallback, this can resurrect deleted objects or leave stale data if legacy is later used.

Delete does not attempt legacy deletion when unified delete returns NotFound

DualWriterMode3.Delete returns immediately on any Storage.Delete error, including NotFound. The previous behavior tolerated NotFound from unified storage and still attempted to delete from legacy storage. With the new behavior, objects that are already absent from unified storage but still present in legacy cannot be cleaned through the API, leaving orphaned legacy data.

Background legacy writes are detached and untracked

Mode 3 launches a new goroutine for every write with no wait group, queue, or shutdown coordination. Destroy can close Storage and Legacy while background writes are still running, which may cause failures or panics if the underlying stores are closed. There is also no backpressure, so a slow legacy backend can cause unbounded goroutine growth.

Asynchronous legacy write failures are not logged

The background create, update, delete, and delete-collection paths only record a metric when the legacy operation fails. They do not log the error or cause. Because these writes are asynchronous and can fail due to cancellation, timeouts, conflicts, or backend errors, operators will have no actionable logs to diagnose legacy divergence.

Mode 3 unit tests do not synchronize or set expectations for async legacy calls

Mode3 methods start goroutines that call LegacyStorage, but the unit tests neither wait for those goroutines nor assert whether legacy was called. For example, TestMode3_Delete calls Delete without setting a Legacy.Delete expectation, so the asynchronous call can hit the mock unexpectedly and race with test completion. Create and Update tests set legacy expectations but never verify them, so they can pass even if the asynchronous legacy write never happens.

Mode 3 integration tests check legacy APIs synchronously despite asynchronous legacy writes

The added mode 3 subtests run doPlaylistTests, which creates, updates, and deletes through the Kubernetes API and then immediately reads the legacy playlist API. In mode 3 the legacy write happens asynchronously, so these checks are racy. Without polling or retry for mode 3, the integration test can flake or hide failures where the legacy write never completes.

Override start and end times are converted to minutes using hour() * 60 + minute() after applying a timezone offset. The checks should compare against the string 'undefined' or use availabilityCheckProps.currentSeats !== undefined directly.

In `searchSupport.init`, each errgroup closure assigns to the outer `err` variable via `_, _, err = s.build(...)` and then returns it. In `server.initWatcher`, the goroutine that pipes backend watch events reads `v := <-events` without checking the channel's ok value and then accesses `v.Type` and `v.ResourceVersion`. `NewResourceServer` creates a cancelable context and then calls `s.Init(ctx)`. ResultsStrategyFactory creates one FixedQueuePool in __init__ (result_consumer.py line 133) and reuses it for every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy. Arroyo closes the old strategy on partition revocation/reassignment, so after a rebalance the factory will create new strategies around an already shut-down pool. New messages then cannot be processed, and enqueue attempts may fail or be dropped. The pool lifecycle must match the strategy lifecycle, or the pool must be recreated on each assignment.

Unbounded worker queues provide no backpressure

Each worker queue is created as queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and FixedQueuePool.submit puts items unconditionally. If workers are slower than the consumer—exactly the slow-item case this PR is trying to address—the consumer will keep polling and enqueuing full Kafka payloads without bound. poll() only emits a gauge and does not block or raise. This can cause unbounded memory growth. Use bounded queues, block in submit, or apply backpressure in poll.

ResultProcessor.__call__ in result_consumer.py also swallows all exceptions and only logs them. The result is that failed results can be committed and never retried, contradicting the strategy docstring claim that offsets are committed only after successful processing. This can silently drop uptime results. Failures should prevent completion, or be routed to retry/DLQ.

submit() marks offsets complete when it cannot enqueue/process a message

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches all exceptions and, if the message has a BrokerValue, immediately adds and completes the offset. This includes decoder/grouping errors and failures from queue_pool.submit, such as submitting to a shut-down queue. The message is not processed, but its offset becomes committable. That turns transient or operational errors into silent data loss. Errors should be surfaced, retried, dead-lettered, or should block the consumer rather than completing the offset.

Concurrent mutation of the partition dictionary can cause RuntimeError during iteration or inconsistent snapshots. Protect the partition set with a global lock, or copy/modify it under a lock.

FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown = True before shutting down the queues, so each worker exits after finishing its current item instead of draining remaining queued work. SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(timeout) calls close() and ignores the timeout, forcibly shutting down the pool. Queued items are dropped on shutdown/rebalance instead of being processed up to the requested timeout. It should wait_until_empty(timeout) and only stop workers after draining or after the timeout expires.

OrderedQueueWorker catches queue.ShutDown, and FixedQueuePool.shutdown calls q.shutdown(immediate=False). These APIs were added in Python 3.13. If this consumer runs on an older supported Python version, shutdown will not work correctly: Queue.shutdown will raise AttributeError (caught and logged), workers may never be woken from queue.get(), and exception handling can fail. Allowlist eligibility is cached for 60 seconds, but invalidate_upsampling_cache is never called when the 'issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist' option changes. If the allowlist is updated, queries can continue using the old upsampling decision for up to a minute, returning incorrect counts. Include a config version in the cache key or invoke invalidation on option changes.

Cache key uses Python hash() of project IDs

The cache key embeds hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids))). Tuple hashes can collide and are not a stable, collision-safe identifier for cached correctness. A collision between different project sets could reuse an eligibility decision for the wrong projects. Use a deterministic unique key such as joined sorted project IDs or a stable hash.

Only literal count() is transformed and aliasing is forced

The transform only rewrites columns that exactly match 'count()' after lower/strip and rewrites them to 'upsampled_count() as count'. It does not handle aliased forms like 'count() as total', other count variants, or equations. This can leave some count aggregations unupsampled while changing the output alias for others, causing inconsistent API responses for clients expecting the original field name.

Allowlist membership check uses list lookups

_are_all_projects_error_upsampled checks 'project_id in allowlist' where allowlist is a list. On a cache miss this is O(number of queried projects * allowlist size). Convert the allowlist to a set before checking membership.

upsampled_count is exposed as a public query function

The new upsampled_count SnQL function is added without private=True, unlike neighboring internal functions. This may allow API callers to invoke it directly in queries, bypassing the allowlist/error-upsampling checks and potentially exposing sample-weight-derived counts. Mark the function private or gate it appropriately.

upsampled_count does not handle missing/null sample weights

The aggregate is toInt64(sum(sample_weight)). If any event in an allowlisted project has a NULL or unpopulated sample_weight (for example historical events before upsampling metadata existed), those events can contribute zero or nothing to the sum, causing severe undercounting. Use coalesce(sample_weight, 1) or another explicit default unless the schema guarantees a non-NULL weight of 1 for every row.

toInt64 truncates fractional upsampled sums

sample_weight values can be fractional, and sum(sample_weight) may therefore be fractional. Wrapping it in toInt64 truncates rather than rounding, biasing the estimated error count downward. Consider rounding or returning a numeric/float result.

Endpoint tests do not clear or test the upsampling eligibility cache

The tests patch the allowlist option but do not clear the 'error_upsampling_eligible:*' cache entries. Since the eligibility cache lives for 60 seconds, a value cached by one test can affect later tests with the same organization/project IDs, making the suite order-dependent and preventing validation of stale-cache behavior. Clear the cache in setUp or add explicit cache invalidation/staleness tests.

Missing coverage for key upsampling paths

The new tests only cover simple stats requests with 'event.type:error'. They do not cover the errors dataset, top-events paths, RPC paths, aliased/equation count columns, dashboard split queries, or mixed/negated event.type queries. These are the paths where the transform is applied and are likely to regress.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

Asynchronous legacy writes are derived from the request context

In Create, and similarly in Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection, the background goroutine creates a timeout context from the incoming request context. Request contexts are normally canceled when the HTTP handler returns, so the 10-second timeout does not make the legacy write independent. The legacy operation may be canceled immediately after the API response is sent, causing mode 3 to skip the intended asynchronous legacy write. A detached context, with logger/values copied, should be used instead.

Mode3.Create passes the original obj to Legacy.Create after Storage.Create has returned created. Storage may assign name, UID, resourceVersion, annotations, or defaults, and created is the canonical object that unified storage accepted. Passing the original object, rather than a deep copy of created, can create a different object in legacy storage or cause concurrent use of a mutable object. This can make legacy storage diverge from unified storage.

Legacy Update reuses the request UpdatedObjectInfo instead of the unified result

Mode3.Update calls Storage.Update with objInfo and then asynchronously calls Legacy.Update with the same objInfo. Legacy.Update will normally evaluate objInfo against the legacy store's current object, so patches, strategic merges, or resource-version-dependent updates can produce a different result or fail. To keep legacy consistent, the legacy update should receive an UpdatedObjectInfo that returns the exact object returned by Storage.Update, preferably a deep copy.

Each write operation starts an independent goroutine to write to legacy storage without sequencing, queueing, or per-resource locking. Rapid create/update/delete operations can be applied to legacy out of order, for example a legacy delete can run before a legacy create or an older update can overwrite a newer one. Because mode 3 keeps legacy as a fallback, this can resurrect deleted objects or leave stale data if legacy is later used.

DualWriterMode3.Delete returns immediately on any Storage.Delete error, including NotFound. The previous behavior tolerated NotFound from unified storage and still attempted to delete from legacy storage. With the new behavior, objects that are already absent from unified storage but still present in legacy cannot be cleaned through the API, leaving orphaned legacy data.

When Storage.Create fails, recordLegacyDuration is called at line 45; when Storage.Update fails, recordLegacyDuration is called at line 129; and the asynchronous Legacy.DeleteCollection result is recorded with recordStorageDuration at line 166. These record the duration or error state of the wrong store, making mode 3 observability misleading.

Background legacy writes are detached and untracked

Mode 3 launches a new goroutine for every write with no wait group, queue, or shutdown coordination. Destroy can close Storage and Legacy while background writes are still running, which may cause failures or panics if the underlying stores are closed. There is also no backpressure, so a slow legacy backend can cause unbounded goroutine growth.

Asynchronous legacy write failures are not logged

The background create, update, delete, and delete-collection paths only record a metric when the legacy operation fails. They do not log the error or cause. Because these writes are asynchronous and can fail due to cancellation, timeouts, conflicts, or backend errors, operators will have no actionable logs to diagnose legacy divergence.

Mode3 methods start goroutines that call LegacyStorage, but the unit tests neither wait for those goroutines nor assert whether legacy was called. For example, TestMode3_Delete calls Delete without setting a Legacy.Delete expectation, so the asynchronous call can hit the mock unexpectedly and race with test completion. In mode 3 the legacy write happens asynchronously, so these checks are racy. Without polling or retry for mode 3, the integration test can flake or hide failures where the legacy write never completes.

useAllRulerRuleAbilities hardcodes isFederated = false, replacing the previous isFederatedRuleGroup check. Federated ruler rule groups should be immutable, but this change makes update, delete, pause, and restore appear supported for them if the user has permissions, regressing UI/RBAC behavior for federated cloud rules.

useCanSilence returns a new [supported, allowed] array on every render, and that tuple is included in the useMemo dependency array of useAllRulerRuleAbilities. The memo therefore recomputes on every render, which can add noticeable overhead when these hooks are invoked for many rows in the rule list.

getGrafanaRuleKey returns a template string ending in ${rule.uid}}, so the generated key contains an unintended trailing closing brace. This does not crash React but makes keys incorrect and can confuse debugging or key-based assumptions.

Clipboard write promise rejection is not handled

copyToClipboard calls navigator.clipboard.writeText(...).then(...) without a catch handler. If the Clipboard API rejects, for example due to browser permissions or an insecure context, the result is an unhandled promise rejection.

Tests named 'Should not render Edit/Delete button for users with the update/delete permission' mock useIsRuleEditable with isEditable or isRemovable true and then assert the buttons are absent, without granting the corresponding permissions. This likely tests the wrong condition and can pass even if the RBAC button visibility logic is broken.

runSplitQuery filters targets on query.expr before calling applyTemplateVariables. If a target's raw expression is a non-empty variable that interpolates to an empty string, it is not discarded. It can then be grouped and sent to Loki as an empty query; if all targets become empty, the grouped requests array is empty and runSplitGroupedQueries can fail (Math.max over an empty array and undefined longest partition). Filter again after interpolation.

Shard splitting now filters empty expressions before interpolation

runShardSplitQuery changed from interpolating targets before filtering out empty expressions to filtering expressions first and interpolating afterwards. A query whose raw expr is a non-empty variable but whose interpolated expression is empty will no longer be discarded. This is a behavior regression and can create invalid shard queries or empty request groups. Add a filter after applyTemplateVariables.

Already interpolated/sharded queries are interpolated again by runSplitQuery

runShardSplitQuery interpolates targets at the start and later calls runSplitQuery for each shard group. runSplitQuery now unconditionally interpolates targets again. The updated tests expect applyTemplateVariables to be called multiple times for one query in the shard flow. Because applyTemplateVariables receives request.filters and template replacement is not necessarily idempotent, repeated interpolation can duplicate ad-hoc filters or alter already-interpolated values containing '$'. This can change or corrupt the shard-modified query. Avoid re-interpolating already interpolated targets or make the operation explicitly idempotent.

There is no transaction, lock, or conditional database operation tying the count check to the write. Concurrent anonymous requests for new devices can all observe count below device_limit and then all insert new rows, causing the number of active anonymous devices to exceed the configured limit.

Once the limit is reached, Anonymous.Authenticate rejects unknown devices, so legitimate new anonymous devices can be denied access. This makes the limit exploitable as a denial-of-service vector.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.

Local cache is populated before persistence, allowing blocked devices to bypass the limit on retry

tagDeviceUI stores the device key in the local cache before calling CreateOrUpdateDevice. If CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, or any other database error, the cache entry is not removed. For the cache TTL, subsequent requests with the same device ID hit the cache and TagDevice returns nil without touching the database, so Anonymous.Authenticate succeeds. A device that was initially rejected by the device limit can therefore retry and bypass the limit, and database failures are also hidden.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: tagDeviceUI caches the device ID before CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds, and leaves the cache entry after ErrDeviceLimitReached, allowing retries to bypass the device limit until expiration. The candidate's additional discussion of database errors does not change the match.

false_positives.candidate:
Device limit can be bypassed by omitting the client-supplied device header

TagDevice returns nil when X-Grafana-Device-Id is empty, and Anonymous.Authenticate only rejects authentication when TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Because the device ID header is supplied by the client, an anonymous client can omit it and avoid being counted or blocked, while normal UI clients that send the header are limited. The configured device_limit therefore cannot reliably cap anonymous devices.

Device tagging is now synchronous on the anonymous authentication path

TagDevice was moved from a background goroutine into Anonymous.Authenticate. When device_limit is non-zero, each uncached device triggers a COUNT query plus a database write before the anonymous identity is returned. This adds latency to anonymous requests and can become a performance hotspot on instances with many anonymous devices.

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only verifies that a second, unknown device is rejected when the limit is 1. It does not verify that an existing active device can still be updated after the limit is reached. Since returning anonymous devices should remain authenticated, a regression in updateDevice could lock out existing devices without being caught.

untagDevice logs the wrong error variable

In untagDevice, when DeleteDevice fails the log statement uses the incoming err variable instead of errD, the error returned by DeleteDevice. As a result, the logged error is unrelated to the actual delete failure.

SimpleRSS.parse open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) uses open-uri without timeouts, redirect controls, or rescue for network and parse errors. A slow, unreachable, or malformed feed can hang or crash the scheduled job.

In the update branch, TopicEmbed.import calls PostRevisor#revise! and then unconditionally updates the embed content_sha1. If the revision/save fails or returns false, the stored SHA will no longer match the post body and future legitimate content changes may be skipped.

After PostCreator#create, TopicEmbed.import checks if post.present?. The subsequent TopicEmbed.create! can then fail on nil topic_id/post_id or create inconsistent data. Check post.persisted? and errors before creating the embed.

TopicEmbed belongs_to :topic and :post but has no dependent destroy or cleanup callback. If a topic or post is destroyed, stale topic_embed rows remain. topic_id_for_embed can then return a deleted topic id, and update code may later call methods on a nil post.

sendAddGuestsEmails does not accept or check event-type email disable settings, unlike other email-sending helpers. Add-guests notifications will be sent even when standard host/attendee emails are disabled for the event type.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that sendAddGuestsEmails fails to honor event-type settings disabling standard emails, causing host/attendee notifications to be sent despite those settings.

false_positives.candidate:
Any attendee can modify the guest list

The permission check treats any attendee whose email matches the authenticated user's email as allowed to add guests. This lets a participant, not just the organizer/host, modify the guest list and trigger invitation emails to arbitrary addresses. Unless this is an explicit product decision, the endpoint should restrict this action to hosts/team admins.

Endpoint does not validate booking status

The handler fetches the booking but never checks its status or timing. The API can therefore add guests to cancelled, rejected, pending, or past bookings even if the UI hides the action. This can send notifications and update calendar events for bookings that should no longer be modified.

No limit on number of guest emails

guests is validated only as an array of email strings with no maximum length. An authenticated user can submit a very large array, causing a large createMany operation and mass email sending. Add a reasonable max length.

Organizer lookup can throw for bookings without a user

The organizer lookup uses `booking.userId || 0` with findFirstOrThrow. If a booking has no userId, for example in some team/round-robin cases, this queries user id 0 and throws a Prisma not-found error, producing a 500 instead of handling the missing organizer.

Attendees are persisted before calendar update without a transaction

Attendees are persisted with prisma.booking.update before calling eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees, and the whole operation is not transactional. If the calendar update fails, guests remain attached to the booking while the client receives an error, leaving Cal.com attendees and external calendar attendees inconsistent.

Invalid-email error state is not reset after successful submission

The mutation success handler closes the dialog and resets the email list but does not reset isInvalidEmail. If a previous submission failed validation and a later submission succeeds, reopening the dialog can still show the stale validation error.

Error toast fallback is never used

The error message is built with a template string that is always non-empty, so the fallback to t('unable_to_add_guests') never runs. Users may see a message like `undefined: ...` when no TRPC error code is present.

To address can be malformed for guests with empty name

New guest attendees are created with an empty name, and the email sets `to` to `${attendee.name} <${attendee.email}>`. This can produce a malformed display name such as ` <guest@example.com>`. Use the email address as a fallback when name is empty.

Hard-coded English tooltip

The remove-email tooltip content is hard-coded as 'Remove email' instead of using the translation hook, so it will not be localized.

No tests for the new add-guests endpoint

No automated tests are added for the new tRPC endpoint, including its permission logic, duplicate/blacklisted email handling, and email selection. These are security-sensitive paths that would benefit from regression tests.

true_positives.golden_comment: Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup-code matching is case- and whitespace-sensitive

Backup codes are generated as lowercase hex strings, but during login they are compared with `indexOf` after only removing dashes. The value is not trimmed or lowercased. A user who enters a valid code in uppercase, which is suggested by the UI placeholder, or with surrounding whitespace will be rejected despite having a valid backup code.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same case-sensitive indexOf comparison that rejects valid backup codes containing uppercase hex characters. Its additional whitespace concern does not change the match.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup-code single-use guarantee is not atomic

After matching a backup code, the code is invalidated by decrypting the stored array, setting the matched entry to null, and writing it back with a separate `prisma.user.update`. This read-modify-write is not transactional or protected against concurrent updates. Two simultaneous login attempts using the same backup code can both read it as unused and both succeed. Concurrent uses of different codes can also overwrite each other's updates and resurrect a previously used code.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify a non-atomic read-modify-write race that allows concurrent login attempts to successfully reuse the same backup code, violating one-time-use semantics. The candidate adds a related lost-update scenario without changing the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup-code login can bypass password verification

In the credentials authorize callback, the password is only verified when `!credentials.totpCode` (line 121). The new backup-code branch at line 131 is entered whenever `credentials.backupCode` is present, even if a non-empty `totpCode` is also supplied. An attacker can send credentials containing any non-empty `totpCode` and a valid backup code; the password check is skipped and the backup code alone authenticates. This turns a backup code into a single-factor credential and allows login without the account password.

Dialog can be dismissed after enabling 2FA without notifying parent or resetting state

After TOTP verification succeeds, the modal switches to the backup-code screen, but `onEnable` and `resetState` are only invoked by the explicit Close button. If the user dismisses the dialog through `onOpenChange` (for example via backdrop click, close icon, or Escape), the parent is not notified that 2FA has been enabled and the modal state is not reset. The settings UI can remain stale until a reload, and sensitive state such as backup codes or object URLs may persist.

Disable endpoint rejects uppercase backup codes

The disable endpoint compares the supplied backup code after removing dashes but without trimming or lowercasing it. Since generated codes are lowercase hex, a valid backup code entered in uppercase or with surrounding whitespace is rejected, preventing a user from disabling 2FA with a valid code.

No tests cover actual backup-code authentication or single-use behavior

The PR adds a security-critical backup-code login and disable flow, but the e2e tests only verify that backup codes can be downloaded, copied, and closed. There is no test that logs in with a backup code, disables 2FA with a backup code, or asserts that a consumed backup code cannot be reused, so the core feature and its single-use guarantee are untested.

false_positives.candidate:
TypeError when destinationCalendar is empty and location is Google Meet

In EventManager.create, mainHostDestinationCalendar is destructured from evt.destinationCalendar ?? []. If destinationCalendar is null or an empty array, mainHostDestinationCalendar is undefined, but the next line reads mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration without optional chaining. This will throw a TypeError for Google Meet events that have no destination calendar, breaking booking creation.

Video credentialId is no longer stored in references created by EventManager.create

referencesToCreate now sets credentialId only when the result is a calendar result. Previously, non-calendar results preserved result.credentialId. As a result, video booking references can be created with credentialId undefined. Later cancellation or update flows that look up the video credential by reference.credentialId may fail to delete or update the meeting.

Only the first old calendar reference is deleted when merging bookings

When newBookingId is provided, updateAllCalendarEvents deletes the old calendar event by finding only the first booking reference whose type includes _calendar. For collective or multi-host bookings there can be multiple calendar references, so the remaining old calendar events will not be deleted and can remain on host calendars.

Fallback credential filter looks for exact type calendar

createAllCalendarEvents falls back to this.calendarCredentials.filter(cred => cred.type === 'calendar') when no destinationCalendar is present. Calendar credential types are normally values like google_calendar or office365_calendar, so this exact equality will usually match nothing. The stated fallback to the first connected calendar will therefore not create any calendar event.

Possible duplicate creation for other_calendar integrations

createAllCalendarEvents first creates events for each entry in event.destinationCalendar, then unconditionally creates events for every credential whose type includes other_calendar. If a destinationCalendar entry is itself an other_calendar credential, the same integration event can be created twice.

updateLocation can create booking references without credential or external calendar identifiers

updateLocation maps results into referencesToCreate using result.externalId and result.credentialId. Calendar update results from CalendarManager.updateEvent do not populate these fields, so calendar references produced by updateLocation can have undefined credentialId and externalCalendarId. Handlers that persist these references may store incomplete reference rows.

Team destination calendars are dropped when organizer has no destination calendar

For collective team events, evt.destinationCalendar is initialized to null when neither eventType nor organizer has a destinationCalendar. The later call evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars) then does nothing because of optional chaining on null. Hosts' destination calendars are silently lost, so their calendar events may not be created.

Google deleteEvent fallback can target the wrong calendar

deleteEvent now only uses externalCalendarId when provided; otherwise it attempts to find a destination calendar with externalId === externalCalendarId, which is undefined when no externalCalendarId was passed. It then falls back to primary. If the event exists on a non-primary calendar and externalCalendarId is missing, deletion can fail silently with a 404 or leave the event on the correct calendar.

Google event patch can use undefined calendarId

createEvent inserts the event with calendarId selectedCalendar || 'primary', but the subsequent events.patch call uses calendarId: selectedCalendar without the same fallback. If selectedCalendar is undefined, the patch request can fail even though the event was created on primary.

Google createEvent ignores destination externalId when credentialId is absent

createEvent now chooses the Google calendar by finding a destinationCalendar entry with the same credentialId. Older or incomplete destinationCalendar records may have externalId but no credentialId. In that case the service falls back to primary, whereas the previous behavior could use destinationCalendar.externalId. This can create events on the wrong calendar after the migration to arrays.

Lark createEvent only uses the first destination calendar for multi-host events

LarkCalendarService.createEvent destructures the first entry from event.destinationCalendar and ignores the credential that is creating the event. When EventManager creates events for multiple hosts, each host's credential receives the same full destinationCalendar array, but Lark always tries to use the first host's calendar. This can create events on the wrong calendar or fail for other hosts.

CalDAV createEvent only uses the first destination calendar for multi-host events

BaseCalendarService.createEvent filters calendars by the first entry of event.destinationCalendar. It does not select the destination calendar that corresponds to the credential creating the event. With multiple host destination calendars, CalDAV events for non-first hosts can be created on the wrong calendar or fail.

Recurring cancellation only deletes the first calendar reference per booking

When cancelling all remaining recurring bookings, the code finds only the first reference whose type includes _calendar for each updated booking and attempts deletes using the organizer's calendar credentials. Multi-host bookings can have multiple calendar references, including credentials that are not in bookingToDelete.user.credentials, so some host calendar events may not be deleted.

Awaiting the apiDeletes array does not await deletion promises

In the paid cancellation branch, the code executes await apiDeletes where apiDeletes is an array of promises. This does not wait for the promises or catch their rejections. Calendar or video deletions may still be running when the handler returns, and failures will not be handled by the surrounding try/catch.

Confirming a pending collective booking only includes one destination calendar

confirmHandler builds evt.destinationCalendar from only booking.destinationCalendar or user.destinationCalendar. It does not include destination calendars for other collective hosts. When a pending collective booking is confirmed, EventManager.create will therefore only create the organizer's calendar event, not events for all hosts.

Webhook payload destinationCalendar is inconsistent between events

The test expects destinationCalendar to be [] for BOOKING_REJECTED but expects null for BOOKING_CREATED and BOOKING_REQUESTED elsewhere in the same file. The migration to an array-backed destinationCalendar should use a consistent empty representation across webhook payloads to avoid breaking consumers.

Dynamic import failures in getCalendar reject instead of returning null

getCalendar now awaits appStore[...] but does not catch errors from the dynamic import. Previously an unknown or unavailable calendar type could return null after a warning; now a rejected import throws. Callers such as CalendarManager.getCachedResults use Promise.all over getCalendar, so one broken app can fail all calendar availability requests. Wrap the import lookup in try/catch and return null, or otherwise handle the failure.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify unhandled failures from the awaited dynamic import and recommend try/catch to handle those failures gracefully. The candidate adds caller-impact details but describes the same underlying issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Async forEach does not await calendar/video deletions

bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => ...) starts asynchronous getCalendar/deleteEvent/deleteMeeting operations, but Array.prototype.forEach does not wait for the callbacks' promises. The surrounding try/catch will not catch rejections, and Reschedule can send the reschedule email and return before the external events are deleted. Use Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...)) or a for...of loop with await.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same async-forEach bug: callback promises are not awaited, surrounding try/catch cannot catch their rejections, and execution can proceed before cleanup completes. It also recommends the same fixes, Promise.all with map or an awaited for...of loop.

false_positives.candidate:
All app-store imports are started eagerly, not lazily

The appStore object initializes every entry with import(...) at module load. Importing appStore therefore starts loading every app chunk, even if only one integration is used. This defeats much of the benefit of async imports and can increase startup/network cost. It also creates many promises that may never be awaited; if one dynamic import fails and that app is never used, the rejection may become unhandled. A lazy getter or function that imports only the requested app would be safer.

Reschedule mutation fires calendar/video deletions without awaiting them

bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => ...) performs awaited getCalendar and returns deleteEvent/deleteMeeting promises, but forEach ignores those promises. The mutation can complete, send emails, and call webhooks before external calendar/video events are deleted, and any deletion failure becomes an unhandled promise rejection. Use Promise.all or a for...of loop and await the deletions.

Async forEach can leave apiDeletes unpopulated and unawaited

The recurring-calendar cancellation branch uses .forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); ... apiDeletes.push(...) }). Because forEach does not await async callbacks, later code may reach await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes)) before apiDeletes is fully populated, so calendar deletions may not be awaited or may be skipped. Errors from those async callbacks are also unhandled. Use a for...of loop or collect promises with map and Promise.all.

Awaiting the apiDeletes array does not await its promises

In the paid cancellation path, await apiDeletes; awaits the array object, not the promises it may contain. The handler can return before calendar/video deletion promises settle, and rejections from those promises may become unhandled. It should be await Promise.all(apiDeletes), after ensuring apiDeletes is fully populated.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Inconsistent metric tag key: shards vs shard

The wait_produce timer is tagged with `shards`, while the produce timer and segment_size_bytes metric use `shard`. This inconsistency will make metrics harder to query and can silently break dashboards/alerts that expect a single tag name for flusher shard attribution.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same problem: the wait_produce metric is tagged 'shards' while the produce and segment_size_bytes metrics are tagged 'shard'. Both also say this breaks aggregation and dashboards.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() can skip terminating some flusher processes when timeout expires

SpanFlusher.join iterates over multiple flusher processes and breaks out of the loop as soon as the remaining deadline is <= 0. If the deadline is reached before later processes are visited, those processes are never terminated. Also, `deadline = time.time() + timeout if timeout else None` treats timeout == 0 as no deadline, so join can block indefinitely. During shutdown or rebalance this can leave flusher processes running or hang the consumer.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same bug as the golden comment. Breaking out of the loop once the deadline expires skips terminating the remaining flusher processes, leaving them running. The extra point about timeout == 0 is additional and does not change the match.

false_positives.candidate:
Restart path kills unhealthy process but never ensures it has exited

_ensure_processes_alive calls process.kill() for an unhealthy process and immediately creates a replacement without joining or otherwise verifying the old process has exited. The old process object is replaced, which can leak zombie/process resources. If the old worker is not actually dead (or in the thread-based test mode, where threads cannot be killed), two workers may flush the same shards concurrently, risking duplicate Kafka production and confusing buffer state.

Unvalidated --flusher-processes value can crash or silently change behavior

The new --flusher-processes option accepts any integer. A negative value reaches SpanFlusher, where num_processes becomes negative and process_to_shards_map is empty; the subsequent shard assignment then raises KeyError during consumer startup. A value of 0 is silently treated as “use one process per assigned shard” because of `max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`. The option should validate the allowed range or document the sentinel behavior.

Docstring overstates one-process-per-shard behavior

The class docstring says the flusher creates one process per shard, but the implementation creates min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards)) processes and may assign multiple shards to one process. The CLI default is also 1 process, so the documented behavior does not match the default or the configurable behavior.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
zip(error_ids, events.values()) may pair wrong event IDs with wrong data

`nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` returns a dict that may omit missing keys and does not guarantee ordering matches the input list. Using `zip(error_ids, events.values())` will silently pair the wrong event_id with the wrong event data when any node is missing from the result. The correct approach is to iterate over `error_ids` and look up each corresponding node_id in the returned dict.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same bug in the zip(error_ids, events.values()) pairing. They agree that get_multi may not preserve input order and that missing nodes shift the alignment, so event data gets paired with the wrong ID.

The account UI message 'error-invalid-multivalued-size' was changed from i18next-style interpolation ('{{0}}', '{{1}}', '{{2}}') to Java MessageFormat syntax ('{0}', '{2,choice,...}'). The surrounding account-ui messages still use '{{...}}' placeholders and react-i18next/Trans tags such as '<0>', so this value will not be formatted by the UI. Users will likely see the literal pattern, including the raw choice expression, instead of a localized validation message.

Java MessageFormat/choice syntax used in an i18next-based admin UI message

The admin UI message 'error-invalid-multivalued-size' was changed from i18next-style interpolation ('{{0}}', '{{1}}', '{{2}}') to Java MessageFormat syntax ('{0}', '{2,choice,...}'). Admin UI message resources generally use '{{...}}' interpolation, so this key will not be substituted or pluralized client-side. The UI will display the raw MessageFormat/choice pattern instead of a properly formatted error message.

PropertyResourceBundle is constructed from an InputStream and will not read UTF-8 properties reliably

verifySafeHtml() creates PropertyResourceBundle directly from FileInputStream for both the checked file and its English counterpart. PropertyResourceBundle(InputStream) uses the legacy ISO-8859-1 properties encoding, while Keycloak theme message files in this PR contain UTF-8 translated text. Non-ASCII message contents will be mangled before sanitization/comparison, which can cause false positives, false negatives, or confusing verifier diagnostics. Use an InputStreamReader with StandardCharsets.UTF_8 for both bundles.

Lithuanian login message replaced with Italian text

In the Lithuanian login messages file, 'loginTotpStep1' is now 'Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:', which is Italian. The surrounding messages are Lithuanian, so Lithuanian users will see an Italian instruction line during login/OTP setup.

Danish email paragraph starts with stray 'n' character identityProviderLinkBodyHtml contains '

nHvis du ikke vil forbinde disse konti...', where 'nHvis' appears to be a typo for 'Hvis'. Since this line was touched to add the closing '

' tag, the user-visible Danish email text should also be corrected.

HTML detection only matches lowercase tag names HTML_TAGS is '<[a-z]+[^>]*>', so it only detects lowercase HTML tags. If an English source string contains HTML with uppercase or mixed-case tags such as '
' or '', containsHtml() will return false and translations using the same tags will be rejected as illegal HTML even though the source string contains HTML. The tag detection should be case-insensitive or otherwise more robust.

English companion file is derived by regex-replacing the whole absolute path

englishFile is computed by applying replaceAll('resources-community', 'resources') and replaceAll('_[a-zA-Z-_]*\.properties', '_en.properties') to file.getAbsolutePath(). This can alter unrelated parts of a path if they contain those strings and assumes the locale suffix pattern appears only once at the end of the file name. Constructor validates grantType twice instead of rawTokenId

AccessTokenContext's constructor calls Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, 'Null rawTokenId not allowed') instead of checking rawTokenId. A null rawTokenId can therefore be stored and later encoded as the literal string 'null' or produce an invalid token ID. The check should validate rawTokenId, and ideally reject empty values as well.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: the AccessTokenContext constructor checks grantType a second time instead of rawTokenId, so a null rawTokenId passes validation.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId matcher does not validate the expected grant shortcut

AssertEvents.isAccessTokenId uses items[0].substring(3, 5) and returns false when that value equals the expected grant shortcut. The grant shortcut is at zero-based positions 4 and 5, i.e. substring(4, 6), and the condition should reject mismatches. As written, the matcher checks the wrong two characters and inverts the test, so it does not verify the grant shortcut at all. It also calls substring without checking that the prefix is at least six characters, which can throw for malformed IDs.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate flags the same two problems as the golden comment in isAccessTokenId. First, the substring indices are wrong: it should be substring(4,6). Second, the equality check is inverted: it returns false on a match instead of rejecting mismatches. The extra note about a missing length check does not change that the core issue is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Grant shortcuts are not validated for format or null values

DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit reads OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut() and stores it directly in maps. The encoder/decoder assumes every shortcut is exactly two characters, because the token prefix must be six characters total, but there is no validation that shortcuts are non-null, non-empty, exactly two characters, or safely unique. A custom grant factory returning a three-character shortcut, which is encouraged by the OAuth2GrantTypeFactory Javadoc saying '3-letters', will produce token IDs that getTokenContextFromTokenId later rejects. A null shortcut will cause a NullPointerException.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment flags a mismatch between the Javadoc ('3-letters shortcut') and the actual 2-letter shortcuts used in implementations. The candidate explicitly cites this same Javadoc discrepancy: the doc encourages 3 letters while the code assumes exactly 2. Its main framing is missing validation, but it covers the same underlying inconsistency.

false_positives.candidate:
New getShortcut method is a backward-incompatible SPI change

OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is an existing provider-factory interface, and this PR adds an abstract String getShortcut() method without a default implementation. Existing implementations outside this repository will fail to compile and already-compiled implementations can fail at runtime with AbstractMethodError when Keycloak invokes the new method. If this interface is intended to be implemented by extensions, this should be introduced in a compatible way, for example with a default method or explicit migration guidance.

Lazy shortcut map updates bypass duplicate validation and can overwrite mappings

getShortcutByGrantType and getGrantTypeByShortcut lazily insert entries into grantsByShortcuts and grantsToShortcuts when an unknown grant or shortcut is encountered. These lazy updates do not re-run the startup validation for duplicate shortcuts or IDs, so a dynamically available grant with a colliding shortcut can silently overwrite an existing mapping and cause incorrect grant-type resolution. The two maps are also updated separately, so they can be observed in a temporarily inconsistent state.

getTokenContextFromTokenId does not handle null or malformed IDs safely

DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromTokenId immediately calls encodedTokenId.indexOf(':') without checking for null, so a null token ID causes a NullPointerException. It also accepts inputs such as 'onrtac:' and creates a context with an empty raw token ID, because AccessTokenContext does not properly validate rawTokenId. If this method is used to parse token IDs from incoming requests, malformed IDs should result in controlled validation errors rather than NPEs or invalid contexts.

RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential can return a federated credential, but the cleanup calls removeStoredCredentialById, which only removes locally stored credentials.
